---
title: "F3 · Choosing a model"
description: "Pick the cheapest model that clears your quality bar on your own task, and keep the harness that proved it."
---

The model is the most expensive component in most GenAI systems, and the one whose choice moves
quality the most. The rule this book follows everywhere: **choose the cheapest model that clears
your quality bar on your own task, measured on your own examples.** Everything else in this chapter
is how to do that without fooling yourself.

## What the choice actually is

There are three ways to get a model, and within each, a ladder of sizes.

| Option | You pay for | Wins when | Loses when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Proprietary API (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google) | Tokens | You need the strongest models, volume is moderate, you want no GPU operations | Data may not leave your boundary, or volume is so high that tokens cost more than GPUs |
| Hosted open-weight API (Together, Fireworks, Groq) | Tokens, usually cheaper | An open model is good enough and you want API simplicity | You need guarantees on data handling that the provider cannot give, or the model you want is not on their menu |
| Self-hosted open weights | GPU hours and people | Volume is high and steady, or data must stay on your hardware, or you need a fine-tuned model served cheaply | Traffic is spiky or small, or nobody on the team wants to carry a pager for GPUs |

Self-hosting has a break-even point, and it is further out than most teams think once you count
idle capacity and engineering time. [System 39](../systems/39-self-hosted-inference.qmd) works it
out in detail.

Read the table as orders of magnitude rather than as a ranking. The small tier is roughly a

between vendors are smaller than the differences in how many tokens each needs for the same task.

## Choosing, step by step

**1. Write down the bar.** "Good" is not a bar. "At least 90% of answers judged correct and fully
supported by the cited sources, on the golden set" is. If the bar includes latency ("p95 under 3
seconds") or cost ("under $0.01 per request"), write that too.

**2. Build a golden set.** Start with 100 to 300 real examples with known good answers. Real
means drawn from logs, tickets, emails or the people who will use the system, not invented by the
team on a Friday afternoon. [F4](f4-evaluation.qmd) covers how to build it and how big it needs to
be.

**3. Run three to five candidates.** One from each tier, plus the obvious alternatives in the tier
you expect to land in. Use the same prompt, then give each candidate one round of prompt tuning,
because prompts written for one model are rarely optimal for another.

**4. Plot cost against score.** Each candidate is a point. The ones worth considering lie on the
frontier, where no other model is both cheaper and better. Pick the cheapest point above the bar.

**5. Keep the harness.** New models ship every few weeks. With the golden set and the script, a
re-evaluation takes an afternoon. Without them, you are back to reading leaderboards.

## Questions that rule models in or out

Before running any evaluation, these questions often shrink the list:

| Question | Effect |
|---|---|
| Must data stay in a region, or on our hardware? | May rule out vendors without a regional endpoint, or force open weights |
| Does the task need tools, images, audio or very long context? | Rules out models that lack the modality or context length |
| Is a person waiting for the answer? | Rules out slow reasoning settings for the interactive path |
| Do we need to fine-tune? | Pushes towards open weights or vendors that offer tuning on the model you want |
| What happens if this vendor has an outage or changes the price? | Argues for keeping a tested second choice behind a gateway |

## Reasoning effort is a second dial

Current frontier and workhorse models think before answering, and most APIs expose how hard they
think as an effort or budget setting. Thinking tokens are billed as output. That makes effort a
cost dial inside one model: a workhorse model at low effort is often good enough for chat and
extraction, while the same model at high effort handles a coding task. Before building a router
that sends easy requests to a small model and hard ones to a big one, measure the simpler
alternative: one model with effort set per route. One model also means one prompt cache, which
matters more than it looks (see <span class="ocode">O1</span>).

## Mistakes that cost the most

- **Choosing by leaderboard.** Public benchmarks measure someone else's task. They are a filter for
  the shortlist, never the decision.
- **Using the frontier model everywhere.** Classification, routing, extraction and most summarising
  run as well on the small tier at a hundredth of the price. Measure before assuming you need more.
- **Comparing price per token across vendors.** Tokenisers differ. The same prompt can be 20% more
  tokens on one vendor than another. Compare cost per task on your golden set.
- **Upgrading without re-running the evaluation.** A newer model is usually better on average and
  sometimes worse on your task, especially on formatting and instruction-following details your
  parser depends on.
- **Forgetting announced price changes.** Two of the models in the table above have announced
  increases. A cost model built on today's price and deployed for a year should use the price that
  will apply for most of that year.
